newsitem.title: ZAIRE: EU favours closure of Rwanda camps in Zaire -envoy.
newsitem.headline: EU favours closure of Rwanda camps in Zaire -envoy.

text.p: The European Union favours action to close camps in volatile eastern Zaire sheltering more than a million Rwandan refugees, an EU envoy said on Thursday.
Special envoy Aldo Ajello stressed that the EU preferred gradual repatriation of the refugees, who fled civil war and genocide in their homeland in 1994.
But the timing of his statement was bound to please Zaire, which wants Rwandans to go home sooner rather than later.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo reiterated on Wednesday that the camps would be closed before Zaire's long-awaited elections, promised by next May. Most refugees feel Rwanda is still unsafe.

"We have to find a way out of the refugee crisis," Ajello, an Italian, told a news conference in the Zaire capital Kinshasa. "The EU's plan supports a gradual shutting of the camps to ensure the return of the refugees to Rwanda."
The EU statement means the West is united in favour of closing the camps, which are at the root of spiralling ethnic violence in the Great Lakes region of Central Africa that also includes Burundi.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher endorsed the camps' closure during a regional tour last week, saying it was safe for the Hutu refugees to go home from Zaire and Tanzania.
But Ajello said the United States wanted refugees moved further inside Zaire and from the tense Rwanda border. Brussels and Washington would harmonise their views in November.
Ajello said the refugees were costing the international community $1 million daily, half of that from EU coffers.
The Hutu army which held sway in Rwanda until mid-1994 and Hutu tribal militias are blamed for the 1994 genocide of up to a million minority Tutsis or their sympathisers.
Hutus, including former soldiers, fled as Tutsis triumphed in civil war following the massacres. They have been reluctant to return to Rwanda for fear of reprisals.
The Zaire government is under domestic pressure to expel the Rwandans. It forcibly repatriated 15,000 in August before it was obliged to stop in the face of an international outcry.
